 Advertisement ACA and Medicare in 2027: What’s changing and how to prepare
 From premiums to prescription coverage, here’s what to review before choosing your health plan.
 Advertisement Updated: 7:26 AM PST Nov 3, 2026 Editorial Standards ⓘ Courtenay Tucker News Video Curation Team Manager ACA and Medicare in 2027: What’s changing and how to prepare
 From premiums to prescription coverage, here’s what to review before choosing your health plan.
 Updated: 7:26 AM PST Nov 3, 2026 Editorial Standards ⓘ Courtenay Tucker News Video Curation Team Manager Now that you know how to choose the best plan for you , it helps to understand the finer details. Here’s a closer look at what’s coming in 2027 to the ACA Marketplace and Medicare, and what it could mean for your budget.
 ACA Marketplace: Higher Premiums and Shifting Subsidies
 Premiums are changing, and so is the financial help many people rely on to afford coverage. ACA insurers have proposed median premium increases averaging 15% for 2027. So far, 29 states and Washington, D.C., have finalized their increases.
What you actually pay depends on your subsidy, which varies with your income and your local plan costs. “It's tied to a benchmark plan in your area. So as the benchmark plan premium changes, so does your subsidy amount. So you have to look at how your net premiums are changing for 2027. In virtually all cases, they will change,” said health policy analyst Louise Norris of healthinsurance.org.
 Advertisement “In virtually all cases, they will change. It might go up or down depending on how that subsidy amount is changing in your area and also depending on your income,” she said.
 Most enrollees get help. Last year, 87% received subsidies to assist with cost. To find out if you qualify visit healthcare.gov. 
 Higher Out-of-Pocket Limits
 For 2027, the maximum annual out-of-pocket limit for an individual marketplace plan rises from $10,600 to $12,000, and to $24,000 for families.
 “They can’t go above $12,000, but they can be below that,” Norris said. “In a lot of cases, you will see increasing deductibles and increasing out-of-pocket costs, but the amount that they change will vary from one plan to another.”
 If Your Plan Is Leaving the Marketplace
 Insurers are leaving ACA marketplaces in more than 20 states , Norris said. If your plan is ending, the marketplace will, in most cases, pick a replacement for you that comes as close as possible to what you had this year.
 “If your plan is ending altogether, you need to just assume you’re shopping from scratch, starting over, looking at all of the available plans, and picking the one that will best meet your needs,” said Norris.
 Waiting has a real cost. People whose plans end have until December 31 to pick a new one, and a special enrollment period in the first two months of the year offers a do-over for anyone who missed their notice. But the plan the marketplace auto-selects takes effect January 1, while a plan you choose later wouldn’t start until February or March. That switch resets your spending. “If you end up needing care in January and then you pick yourself a different plan in February, you’re starting over at zero out of pocket,” Norris said. That could leave you paying more than the $12,000 individual out-of-pocket maximum in a single year.
 Some Immigrants Lose Subsidy Eligibility
 Another major change: some lawfully present immigrants will no longer qualify for federal marketplace subsidies. That includes people with certain student and work visas, refugees and asylum grantees. “They could still use the marketplace, but they would have to pay full price,” said Norris. An estimated one million people are expected to become uninsured by 2035 as a result of this change.
Immigrants who qualify: 
 Lawful Permanent Resident (LPR)
 Cuba/Haitian Entrant (CHE)
 COFA Migrant
 Immigrants who no longer qualify: 
 Any non-citizens who aren’t in one of the three categories listed above
 Asylees
 Special Immigrant Juvenile and Special Immigrant Visa (Iraq/Afghanistan) 
 Paroled into US
 Granted work permit: EAD
 Conditional entrant before 1980
 Battered spouse, child or parent 
 Family Unity Beneficiary
 Trafficking victim family
 Withholding of deportation or CAT
 VAWA self-petitioner 
 Deferred Enforced Departure
 Refugees
 Tribal member/ American Indian born in Canada 
 Lawful Temporary Resident 
 Temporary Protected Status (TPS) 
 People with various types of temporary visas, such as work visas, student visas, U-visas (for victims of certain crimes) and T-visas (for victims of trafficking). 
 Medicare: Read Your Notice of Change
 The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services reports Medicare Advantage premiums falling about $2 a month on average, while Part D premiums rise about $1. Norris says the averages hide a wider range. “We saw significant increases and significant decreases,” she said. “You certainly should not assume that your plan is going down an average of $2 a month or up an average of $1 a month.”
 Some insurers are shrinking coverage areas or consolidating plans. Norris urges people to read their Annual Notice of Change , mailed by September 30 to Medicare Advantage and Part D enrollees. It shows how your deductible, out-of-pocket exposure, provider network and drug coverage are changing. If you didn’t get one, you may have received a non-renewal notice, which was due by October 2. 
If your Medicare Advantage plan is ending, you can pick another Medicare Advantage plan or move to Original Medicare, with guaranteed access to a Medigap policy , which is not normally available in the fall. Doing nothing is the riskiest choice. “If you are on a Medicare Advantage plan and it is ending and you don’t take any action at all by the end of the year, you will be moved to Original Medicare, but you won’t have any drug coverage or supplemental coverage,” Norris said. A January and February special enrollment period can fix that, but there would be a gap of time before new coverage starts.
 If your plan is staying, don’t assume you can get a Medigap plan if you switch to Original Medicare. Insurers in most states can review your medical history, so Norris recommends talking to them first. The deadline to change plans is December 7.
 The Part D out-of-pocket cap is rising from $2,100 to $2,400. If you take a high-cost drug, you can ask your plan for a payment plan that spreads costs over 12 equal installments of $200. It doesn’t lower your total, but Norris says it helps with budgeting: “It’s easier to budget $200 a month than to spend $2,400 in the first few months of the year.”
 Key Dates and Free Help 
 Medicare 
 Oct. 15–Dec. 7, 2026: Medicare open enrollment. Norris recommends making your choice by Dec. 7.
 Jan. 1–Feb. 28, 2027: Special enrollment period for people whose Medicare Advantage plan ended and who didn’t pick a new one.
 ACA Marketplace 
 Nov. 1, 2026: Marketplace open enrollment begins in most states.
 Dec. 15, 2026: Deadline to choose an ACA marketplace plan that starts Jan. 1, 2027. Norris says every state allows at least until this date.
 Dec. 31, 2026: Deadline to pick a new plan if your current one is ending.
 Jan. 15, 2027: Marketplace open enrollment ends in most states. (A plan chosen after Dec. 15 starts later and out-of-pocket costs don’t carry over.)
 Jan. 1–Feb. 28, 2027: Special enrollment period for people whose ACA plan ended. A plan picked then starts in February or March. 
 Free help 
 Visit HealthCare.gov or your state’s marketplace to compare plans with your 2027 subsidy factored in.
 Medicare beneficiaries can get free, unbiased counseling through SHIP , the State Health Insurance Assistance Program.
